sections.figure_alt: A diagonal 2 by 2 matrix with diagonal entries 6 and -8.
sections.body_md:
The Frobenius norm treats a matrix as a long vector. Square every entry, add, and take the square root. The same number has a singular-value form: square the singular values, add, and take the square root. The two descriptions agree because the squared Frobenius norm equals the sum of the squares of the singular values.

Schatten norms apply an \(\ell_p\) norm to the list of singular values. The Schatten 2-norm is the Frobenius norm. The Schatten 1-norm is the nuclear norm, the sum of the singular values. The Schatten infinity-norm is the spectral norm, the largest singular value, which is also the induced 2-norm.

These are nested. The largest singular value cannot exceed the Euclidean norm of the list, and the Euclidean norm cannot exceed the sum. So the spectral norm is at most the Frobenius norm, which is at most the nuclear norm. Equality holds throughout when the matrix has at most one positive singular value.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[
\lVert A \rVert_F = \sqrt{\sum_{ij} a_{ij}^2} = \sqrt{\sum_i \sigma_i^2}.
\]
The Schatten \(p\)-norm is \(\bigl(\sum_i \sigma_i^p\bigr)^{1/p}\) for \(1 \le p < \infty\), and the largest singular value when \(p = \infty\). In particular the nuclear norm is \(\sum_i \sigma_i\) and the spectral norm is \(\sigma_{\max}(A)\). For every real matrix, \(\lVert A \rVert_2 \le \lVert A \rVert_F \le \lVert A \rVert_{S_1}\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Let \(A = \mathrm{diag}(6, -8)\). The singular values are the absolute diagonal entries 6 and 8. The Frobenius norm is \(\sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100}\), so the Frobenius norm is 10. The nuclear norm is 14, the sum of those singular values. The spectral norm is 8.

The negative sign on the second diagonal entry never enters these three numbers. Using \(6 + (-8)\) would not be a Schatten norm. The gap between 8, 10, and 14 is the usual strict nesting for a matrix with two positive singular values.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The nuclear norm adds singular values. It does not add signed eigenvalues, and it does not add absolute entries of a matrix that is not already diagonal in a singular-vector basis. The spectral norm is not the spectral radius unless the matrix is symmetric, in which case the two agree after absolute values. For a nonsymmetric matrix the spectral radius can be smaller than every singular value. Leaving out the square root in the Frobenius formula produces the square of the norm.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A linear least-squares residual is a Euclidean length of a vector of errors, which is a Frobenius norm when the residual is written as a matrix. The induced 2-norm remains the operator size, and the comparison \(\lVert A \rVert_2 \le \lVert A \rVert_F\) lets an entrywise calculation stand in for that operator size when a rough bound is enough. The nuclear norm is the Schatten norm that penalizes every singular value, not only the largest.
